inline.s: there are Ganges rivers such as these

(The Liushu, the Song canon, the Zhang copy and the Hui edition are all the same. In the circulating edition above 'such' [deng] there is the character 'sand' [sha]. The Southern Tang stone print and the Ming-Qing editions are likewise.)
the past mind is unattainable, the present mind is unattainable, the future mind is unattainable

(The ancient and modern editions are all the same. Only the Hui edition has first 'past', second 'future', third 'present' — and the Asanga bodhisattva's treatise is likewise. The treatise says: 'Because the past is already extinguished; because the future is not yet existent; because the present is of supreme truth.')
the Tathagata should not be seen by the form body

(The Liushu and the Hui edition are the same. In the circulating edition above 'form body' there are the two characters 'fully endowed' [juzu]. The Southern Tang stone print and the editions after are all so.)
then it is slandering the Buddha
(The ancient and modern editions are all the same. In the Southern Tang stone print and the Zhang copy the 'namely' is written 'then'.)
From 'At that time, Subhuti, the life of wisdom' to 'is named beings'

(The Liushu does not have it. The Southern Tang stone print and after have it. These sixty-two characters are absent from the Kumarajiva translation and were added on the basis of the Bodhiruci translation. Therefore the Zhao commentary and even the Essential Selections do not explain them; only the Eulogistic Commentary quotes the Bodhiruci translation in adding and explaining them. Probably in the Tang period they were sometimes added and sometimes not; and after the Five Dynasties, there is none that does not add them. In sum, the meaning of this passage is present in both the verse and the treatise. To take the Bodhiruci translation and add it in is also good. The Kumarajiva translation is likely because the preceding text already has 'the Tathagata speaks of all beings as not beings,' so here it is abridged.)
is it because of nothing attained? So it is, so it is

(The Liushu and the Hui edition are the same. In the circulating edition above 'thus' there is 'the Buddha said.' According to the Southern Tang stone print, the two characters 'the Buddha said' are already present.)
then attaining anuttara samyaksambodhi
the Tathagata speaks of them as not good dharmas

(The Liushu, the Song canon, the Zhang copy and the Hui edition are all the same. In the circulating edition beneath 'speaks' there is the character 'namely'. The Southern Tang stone print and the Ming-Qing editions are all so. The old commentaries such as the Hui commentary and the Eulogistic Commentary, when citing the sutra, all have no character 'namely'; only the Essential Selections quotes it as 'namely not'.)
uphold it and speak it for others
(The Liushu and the Hui edition are the same; the circulating edition beneath 'uphold' has the two characters 'recite' [dusong], and the Southern Tang stone print and the editions after are all so.)
then the Tathagata has self, person, beings, a life span
then it is not having a self
(Same as above.)
then he is not an ordinary person

(Same as above. Also the early Qing edition and the present circulating edition have beneath this sentence another sentence, 'this is named an ordinary person.' The Liushu through the Ming engraving, the Hui commentary, the Zhao commentary, the Master Zhi commentary, the Eulogistic Commentary, and the four-recension edition all do not have it. Some early Qing editions note that it is absent from the old editions. Examining all the old commentaries in detail, none has the meaning of the sentence of naming.)
the wheel-turning sage king is then the Tathagata
if you have this thought, one who arouses anuttara samyaksambodhi

(The Liushu, the Hui edition and the Zhao edition are all the same. In the circulating edition above 'one who' there is the character 'mind', and the Southern Tang stone print and the editions after are all so.)
one who arouses anuttara samyaksambodhi does not speak of an annihilating mark in dharmas
with the seven treasures filling worlds as many as the sands of the Ganges, giving

(The Liushu and the Hui edition are the same. In the circulating edition above 'giving' there are the two characters 'using to hold' [chiyong]. The Southern Tang stone print and the editions after are all so; some Ming engravings, however, lack the two characters 'using to hold'.)
this bodhisattva surpasses the merit gained by the former bodhisattva; Subhuti, because the bodhisattvas do not receive the reward

(The Liushu, the Zhang copy, the Hui commentary, the Eulogistic Commentary and the two-recension edition are all the same. In the circulating edition beneath 'merit' there are the three characters 'for what reason' [he yi gu]. The Southern Tang stone print and the Qisha canon are likewise; some Ming engravings lack the sentence 'for what reason'.)
is this mass of fine dust many? Very many, World-Honored One

(The Liushu, the Song canon, the Ming engraving, the Hui commentary and the other five-recension editions are all the same. In the circulating edition above 'very many' there is the sentence 'Subhuti said.' The Southern Tang stone print, the Zhang Chuliao copy and the early Qing edition all have it.)
then the Buddha does not speak of this mass of fine dust
then it is not a mass of fine dust

(The Liushu, the Song canon, the Zhang copy, the Ming engraving, the Hui commentary and the other five-recension editions are all the same. In the circulating edition the 'then' is written 'namely'; the Southern Tang stone print and the early Qing edition are all so.)
then it is not a world
if a world truly exists
(The Liushu is thus. The Hui commentary recension reads 'has truly'. The circulating edition and the editions after the Southern Tang stone print all read 'truly has' [shi you zhe].)
then it is a combined form

(The Liushu, the Weng copy, the Song canon, the Ming engraving, the Hui commentary and the other five-recension editions are all the same. In the Zhang Chuliao copy, the early Qing edition and the circulating edition the 'then' is written 'namely'.)
then it is not a combined form

(The Liushu, the Song canon, the Zhang copy, the Ming engraving, the Hui commentary and the other five-recension editions are all the same. In the Southern Tang stone print, the early Qing edition and the present circulating edition the 'then' is written 'namely'.)
then it is inexpressible

(The Liushu through the Ming engraving and the Hui commentary and the other five-recension editions are all the same. In the early Qing edition and the present circulating edition the 'then' is written 'namely'.)
does this person understand the meaning I have spoken? World-Honored One

(The Liushu and the Hui edition are the same. In the circulating edition beneath 'not' there is the sentence 'not so' [bu ye]. The editions after the Southern Tang stone print are all so; only the Ming engraving lacks it.)
namely not the view of self, the view of others, the view of beings, the view of a life span
(The ancient and modern editions are all the same; only the Ming engraving writes 'then' for 'namely'.)
the one who arouses the bodhisattva mind

(The Liushu through the Ming engraving and the Hui edition are all the same. In the circulating edition and the early Qing edition the 'bodhisattva' is written 'bodhi'. According to the Changshui record: 'The one who arouses the bodhisattva mind — this singles out the others.')
End of the Collation Notes on the Diamond Sutra
